params.text:
Introduction 

Today’s research world involves considerable complexity – in the number and types of actors involved, and in the relations between them; in the sensitive areas of research undertaken; in the specialization of scientific expertise; in the proliferation of scientific methodologies in different disciplines. This conflict in perspectives, and multitude of competiting interests, often entails conflicts of interest. 

A conflict of interest (COI) exists when an individual or organization has competing interests—financial, personal, or professional—that could undermine their primary duties (e.g. research integrity). 

In many cases, conflicts of interest have an actual impact on the integrity of the research output. In many other cases, the main negative impact is on public trust: even if a research study was not influenced, the failure to disclose certain relations, or funding sources might undermine confidence in the result, or even more broadly undermine confidence in science. This observation further underlines the need for ethical rules and practices concerning conflicts of interest. 

Target audience 

These groups will benefit from tailored, accessible content that enhances their knowledge, compliance practices, and decision-making abilities in research ethics, contributing to a more inclusive and responsible research community.

params.text:
Purpose of module 

The primary purpose of this module is to foster awareness, ethical discernment, and policy literacy around conflicts of interest in research —thus empowering both researchers and ethics reviewers to recognize, disclose, and manage COIs in a transparent and responsible manner. 

Specifically, the course aims to:

  • Bridge the knowledge gap between ethics committee oversight and real world researcher experiences.
  • Promote a culture of integrity, openness, and accountability in all stages of research—from design to dissemination.
  • Offer case-based learning to explore real-life dilemmas, and present clear guidelines for navigating complex ethical terrain.
  • Help institutions and individuals anticipate risks, interpret policies, and respond proactivelyto COI scenarios across disciplines.

Learning objectives 

The purpose of this module is to equip participants with practical knowledge and tools to:
Clearly articulate what constitutes a COI in research, distinguish between financial, non financial, perceived, and actual conflict, explain the ethical and legal implications of unmanaged COIs.

panels.title: Define and Differentiate Conflicts of Interest:

params.text: Recognize common COI scenarios in funding, authorship, peer review, data access, and dissemination; understand COI risks in interdisciplinary and high-stakes fields (e.g., AI ethics, pharma, defense, policy research).

panels.title: Identify COI Risks Across Research Stages:

params.text: Navigate institutional, national, and international guidelines (e.g., ICMJE, NIH, APA, WHO). Understand responsibilities under research ethics regulations and institutional COI disclosure requirements.

panels.title: Interpret Relevant Policies, Guidelines, and Laws:

params.text: Use disclosure forms and management plans appropriately. Evaluate case studies to decide when to recuse, report, or restructure a research role. Recommend institutional safeguards (e.g. firewalls, independent oversight).

params.text:
Identification and Typology of Actor in Potential Conflicts of Interest

In the image below, click on each icon to learn more about the different types of actors commonly involved in potential conflicts of interest.

Actors #1: Funders 

Funding can be public, private or mixed 

  • Commercial bias: A business (e.g. a pharmaceutical or tech company) which funds research that could benefit its product line may – directly or indirectly -- influence the study design or input publication bias.
  • Mission-driven bias: Nonprofits or advocacy groups with ideological agendas (e.g. in behavioral sciences), but also public entities may implicitly push for results that support their views.
  • Conditional funding: Grants contingent on favorable outcomes or subject to non-disclosure agreements.
  • Publication rights: Funders requiring veto power over publication or setting conditions as to publication.

Actors #2: Advisors, Consultants, or Expert Witnesses 

  • Dual roles: Advisors with equity in companies that could benefit from the research.
  • Consulting contracts: Researchers receiving payments from entities that are also stakeholders in the research.
  • Honoraria and speaking fees: Subtle pressures from sponsors via speaking engagements that influence research emphasis or interpretation.

Actors #3: End Users 

Policymakers

Businesses or business groups (health providers; tech Companies)

Non-profit organizations

  • Regulatory capture: Research aligned to anticipated preferences of policy bodies or regulators.
  • Clinical implementation pressure: In life sciences, pressure to produce actionable or cost-effective results for hospitals or payers.
  • Tech alignment: Designing algorithms or systems that favor certain user ecosystems or platforms.

Actors #4: Sponsors or Service/Logistics 

Providers Potential Conflicts: 

  • Data handling bias: External companies managing data collection or analysis may introduce bias or prioritize speed/cost over rigor.
  • Contractual obligations: Sponsors may impose limitations on methods, data access, or publication.
  • Intellectual property ownership: Restrictions on sharing data or code due to service contracts or IP clauses.

Actors #5: Research Institutions 

  • Tech transfer offices: Pressures to commercialize findings, potentially distorting research goals.
  • University investments: Institutions holding equity in startups or products under study.
  • Hiring or promotion bias: Academic incentives that reward high-impact publications over rigorous but null results.
  • Conflict (notably as to intellectual property) between the interests of the institution and the expectations of individual members of its staff

Actors #6: Publishers, journals and review processes 

Peer Review 

Editorial Bias

  • Reviewer-competitor dynamic: Suppressing or delaying rival work through gatekeeping.
  • Editorial preferences: Journals preferring novel or positive results, encouraging data dredging or selective reporting.

Data and Platform Dependencies

  • Platform lock-in: Studies dependent on data from proprietary platforms (e.g. social media APIs) may be limited in critique or reproducibility.
  • AI model bias: Use of pre-trained models from corporations with embedded biases or commercial interests.

params.text:
Example 1: Life Sciences

(Biomedical, Pharmaceutics, Public Health)

Key Conflicts of Interest (COIs):

  • Pharmaceutical funding: Clinical trials funded by drug companies may lead to biased reporting, selective outcome measures, or underreporting of side effects.
  • Ghostwriting and authorship: Medical papers authored by pharmaceutical employees but credited to academics.
  • Diagnostic innovation: Researchers inventing diagnostic tools (e.g., genetic markers) may hold patents or have startup equity.
  • Influence on medical guidelines: Researchers on clinical panels may have undisclosed ties to drug or device companies.

Examples:

  • The Vioxx scandal (Merck) where cardiovascular risks were allegedly downplayed.
  • Gene therapy trials with hidden financial ties between investigators and biotech firms.

answers.text: A pharmaceutical company funding a trial that benefits its own product
A student project with open data access

params.text:
Example 2: Information Technology

(AI, Data Science, Cybersecurity)

Key COIs:

  • Algorithmic bias: Companies funding AI ethics research may suppress f indings that expose bias or harm in their systems.
  • Dual-use technology: Research for facial recognition or surveillance funded by government or defense agencies.
  • Platform access: Dependence on tech giants (Google, Meta) for data access can restrict critical analysis or replication.
  • Consulting roles: Researchers advising both companies and regulators, potentially steering policy toward industry preferences.

Examples:

  • AI ethics researchers dismissed after publishing critical work (e.g. Google and the firing of Timnit Gebru).
  • Bias in commercial LLMs being under-investigated due to conflicts from researchers tied to vendors.

answers.text: A university study independently funded by a public grant
A tech company sponsoring research on its own AI system’s fairness
An open-source community developing a free software library

params.text:
Example 3: Social and Behavioral Sciences

Key COIs:

  • Advocacy-driven funding: Research funded by political, religious, or social interest groups may push ideological outcomes.
  • Government or military influence: Behavioral research used for surveillance, crowd control, or propaganda.
  • Conflict in replication studies: Pressure to produce novel findings over replications can distort the research agenda.
  • Community impact bias: Working with marginalized populations where researchers have implicit financial/career interest in maintaining "researchable" conditions.

Examples:

  • Studies in behavioral economics funded by policy think tanks with clear ideological goals.
  • Social psychology studies incentivized to create “sexy” findings for TED Talks, media, or bestselling books.

answers.text: A study on voter behavior funded by a political organization
A psychology student conducting a class experiment for learning
An independent researcher using open government data

params.text:
Key Practices:

  • Mandatory COI statements in publications, presentations, and funding applications.
  • Public registries for funding sources and investigator affiliations.
  • Clinical trial registration (pre-specifying endpoints and protocols).

Example:
Open Payments Database (U.S.): Tracks payments from drug and device companies to physicians and researchers.

Key Practices:

  • Firewalls between funders and researchers: No influence over study design or publication.
  • Independent data monitoring committees in clinical trials.
  • Ethics boards without institutional ties to funders or sponsors.

Example:
NIH's requirement for independent data safety monitoring boards (DSMBs) in certain trials.

Key Practices:

  • Reward replication and null results through funding and publishing incentives.
  • Academic promotion policies based on transparency, rigor, and impact—not just quantity or novelty.
  • Open science practices (preregistration, data/code sharing, open peer review).

Example:
Some journals and funders (e.g., the Center for Open Science) offer badges or extra credit for reproducibility practices.

Key Practices:

  • Independent audit bodies for COI management.
  • Whistleblower protections for researchers raising COI concerns.
  • Community advisory boards for participatory research, especially in social/behavioral sciences.

Key Practices:

  • Training early-career researchers on ethical dimensions of COIs.
  • Cultivating norms where disclosure is seen as integrity, not shame.
  • Encouraging inter-disciplinary and international collaboration to balance narrow interests.
